sentences.text: Dr.A.K.JAYASANKARAN NAMBIAR, J.

This writ appeal impugns the judgment dated 03.06.2019 of a learned Single Judge in WP(C)
No.8157 of 2017.
2.
The brief facts necessary for disposal of the writ appeal are as follows:
The appellant is stated to be the owner in possession of a total extent of 11.5 cents of land in Re.Sy.No.86/3B.

She had approached the writ court challenging the land acquisition proceedings initiated against her in terms of the Land Acquisition Act,
1894.

It is not in dispute that Section 4(1) notification under the said Act was issued on 04.01.2007 and an award passed on 09.01.2009.
3.

The case of the appellant before the writ court was essentially that, inasmuch as there was no compensation deposited before the court below or possession of the land taken from the appellant on or before 01.01.2014, the date of coming into force of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (hereinafter referred Kavinisseri Chandramathi Amma vs State Of Kerala on 9 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166291496/
2 to as the 2013 Act), the land acquisition proceedings initiated under the 1894 Act had to be seen as lapsed in the light of the specific provisions of Section 24 of the 2013 Act.

entities.text: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
entities.label: STATUTE

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The learned Single Judge, who considered the matter, found that the provisions of Section 24(2)
of the 2013 Act would not be attracted to the facts of the appellant's case, since the award was passed in terms of the 1894 Act on 09.01.2009, which was not beyond the period of five years or more, prior to the commencement of the 2013 Act.
The writ petition was, accordingly, dismissed by the learned Single Judge and the appellant was given one month's time to surrender possession of the building.
The respondents were also given the liberty to take physical possession of the building and land.

5. In the appeal before us, the contentions of the learned counsel for the appellant,
Sri.G.S.Reghunath are premised primarily on the interpretation of the provisions of Section 24(2) of the Act as noticed in the judgment of the Supreme Court in Pune Municipal Corporation v.
Harakchand Misirimal Solanki [2014 (1) KLT 470].

entities.text:
Pune Municipal Corporation v.
Harakchand Misirimal Solanki [2014 (1) KLT 470]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: By placing reliance of the above decision, he would submit that the provisions of Section 24(2) have to be read in the light of the clarification offered by the Supreme Court through a Constitution Bench judgment reported in Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal and others [(2020) 8 SCC 129].

entities.text: Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal and others [(2020) 8 SCC 129]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Therein the Supreme Court had clarified that the word "or" used in Section 24(2) between the two conditions in the second limb of Section 24(2) had to be read as "nor" or as "and" on the reasoning that where two 2025:KER:50511 negative conditions or two prohibitions are coupled by the word "or", the said "or"
has to be read as "and" or "nor".

It is contention of the learned counsel, therefore, that inasmuch as in the instant case neither the taking of possession nor the payment of compensation had occurred prior to the coming into force of the new Act, the provisions of Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act would come into play and the respondents are obliged to continue with the acquisition proceedings in terms of the 2013 Act.

6. Per contra, it is the submission of the learned Senior Counsel, Sri.Gracious Kuriakose, appearing for the respondent Municipality and Sri.T.K.Shajahan, the learned Government Pleader appearing for the State that the instant is a case, where the provisions of Section 24(2) are not attracted at all.

It is pointed out that since the notification under Section 4(1) was issued as early as on 04.01.2007 and the award passed on 09.01.2009 in terms of the 1894 Act, the qualifying period of "five years or more prior to the commencement of this Act" mentioned for the applicability of Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act would not be satisfied.
7.
On a consideration of the rival submissions, we find ourselves in agreement with the submissions of the learned Senior Counsel and the Government Pleader appearing on behalf of the respondents.

Section 24 of the 2013 Act reads as follows:
24. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act in any 2025:KER:50511 case of land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894,--

sentences.text:
3 (a) where no award under Section 11 of the said Land Acquisition Act has been made,
then, all provisions of this Act relating to the determination of compensation shall apply; or (b) where an award under said Section 11 has been made, then such proceedings shall continue under the provisions of the said Land Acquisition Act, as if the said Act has not been repealed.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), in case of land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, where an award under the said Section 11 has been made five years or more prior to the commencement of this Act but the physical possession of the land has not been taken or the compensation has not been paid the said proceedings shall be deemed to have lapsed and the appropriate Government, if it so chooses, shall initiate the proceedings of such land acquisition afresh in accordance with the provisions of this Act:
Provided that where an award has been made and compensation in respect of a majority of land holdings has not been deposited in the account of the beneficiaries,
then, all beneficiaries specified in the notification for acquisition under Section 4 of the said Land Acquisition Act, shall be entitled to compensation in accordance with the provisions of this Act.
8.

The Supreme Court in Indore Development Authority (supra) has clarified that the disjunctive portion of the second limb of section 24(2) of the 2013 Act has to be read as conjunctive and that the word "or" used in the second limb should be read as "and" or "nor" for the purposes of sub section (2) of that section.

We find, however, that the instant is a case where the acquisition from the appellant would not fall within the first limb of Section 24(2) since the award in the instant case was passed within the period of five years prior to the 2025:KER:50511 commencement of the 2013 Act.
As already noticed above, the award was passed on 09.01.2009 and the new Act came into force with effect from 01.01.2014.
The provisions of Section 24(2) would have been attracted only if the award was passed prior to 01.01.2009.

That not being the case in the present appeal, we find that it is the provisions of Section 24(1)(d) that would be attracted, enabling the respondents to continue the proceedings initiated against the lands of the appellant under the provisions of the 1894 Act, as if the said Act had not been repealed.
We, therefore, see no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment of the learned Single Judge.
The appeal fails, and is, accordingly, dismissed.
